notes:
Finding 1 (OfficialNumberService INSERT race): widened the bounded retry's catch from `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` only to also catch a plain `DbUpdateException` wrapping a `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteException` with SqliteErrorCode 19 (SQLITE_CONSTRAINT) via a new `IsSequenceRaceException` helper. Recovery is a single unified `db.Entry(row).ReloadAsync(...)` call for both cases (no detach branch needed): re-querying by the (Kind, Year) key after either failure type refreshes the tracked row from the now-current DB state and flips an Added-but-failed entry to Unchanged once the reload finds the real row, so the next attempt updates it instead of re-inserting. On the final (Nth) exhausted attempt, the exception is now run through the newly-injected `IErrorMapper` (added as a third constructor dependency, already registered as a singleton in `AddWakeelCore`, so no DI wiring changes were needed) and re-thrown as an `InvalidOperationException` carrying the mapped reference id, so a raw `DbUpdateException`/`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` never escapes untranslated.

Testing note (materially informs anyone touching this again): I verified empirically (via a throwaway console probe against the built assembly, not committed) that on this SQLite/WAL configuration (journal_mode=WAL, busy_timeout=5000, SQLCipher, `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite`), two *genuinely overlapping* `Database.BeginTransactionAsync()` transactions cannot coexist — the second's BeginTransactionAsync call itself blocks (and eventually times out with SQLITE_BUSY/'database is locked') even if the first transaction has only read so far. This holds even under `IsolationLevel.ReadUncommitted`; that isolation level does let one side's write commit while the other's still-open, read-only transaction persists, but the read-only side's own *subsequent* write then hits SQLITE_BUSY (a WAL busy-snapshot condition) rather than a UNIQUE-constraint violation, and retrying within that same transaction never recovers (proven: a hook-based live-race attempt exhausted all 5 retries, every one busy). Consequently, the literal 'two contexts both concurrently see no row and race to insert' scenario cannot be reproduced through two truly-overlapping ambient transactions on this stack; it always resolves earlier as a busy/locked condition that a same-transaction retry cannot fix. The committed regression test (`Issue_WhenAnotherContextInsertedTheVeryFirstRowFirst_IsRetried_AndTheNumbersDiffer`) instead engineers the exact downstream symptom deterministically and without any timing dependency: it tracks a new (Added, unsaved) `OfficialNumber` on a second `DbSession`'s context — precisely the in-memory state IssueCoreAsync's own first attempt would leave — then lets an entirely separate, ordinary transaction (via `_service`/`_session`) fully insert and commit the real first row. When the second context then opens its own (now perfectly ordinary, non-overlapping) transaction and calls `IssueAsync`, EF's identity resolution hands back its already-tracked Added instance instead of a fresh materialization of the real row, so the service's own SaveChanges genuinely hits SQLITE_CONSTRAINT (19) on the real row that now exists, and the fixed retry logic reloads and succeeds with the next sequence number, distinct from the winner's. This is deterministic (ran 4x back-to-back with zero flakes) and exercises the exact new catch/reload code path, though the precise mechanism used to reach it (a pre-tracked entity) is a test-only construction rather than a live two-thread race, since a live race on this engine cannot reach the same code path.

Finding 2 (DateTimeConverterTests precondition race): replaced the racy `Assert.Empty(logger.Warnings)` precondition in `Read_UnparseableText_IsForwardedToTheContextLoggerAsAWarning` with `Assert.DoesNotContain(logger.Warnings, w => w.Contains(corrupt, StringComparison.Ordinal))`, matching the filtering pattern already used by every other assertion against the process-wide `DataIntegrityLog.Reported` event in this file.

No new NuGet packages were added (Microsoft.Data.Sqlite was already a transitive/available namespace via the existing Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Core package reference, already used elsewhere in Wakeel.Core, e.g. DbConnectionFactory.cs and ErrorMapper.cs). No files outside src/Wakeel.Core and tests/Wakeel.Core.Tests were touched (verified via `git diff --stat` and that no other project directly constructs `OfficialNumberService` — all other consumers go through DI, unaffected by the added `IErrorMapper` constructor parameter). Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props, Wakeel.slnx and docs/ were not touched. No git commit/checkout/stash/reset was run; all changes are left in the working tree. Full suite run 4x back-to-back (171/171 green each time) to confirm no flakiness was introduced.
